section: Right to Constitutional Remedies - Article 32; the five writs and their scope
subsections: Articles 29-30 - language, script, culture, minority educational institutions

accepted.s:
With reference to Article 29 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
1. Any section of citizens having a distinct language, script or culture has the right to conserve it.
2. Article 29 is confined exclusively to religious and linguistic minorities.
3. No citizen can be denied admission to a State-maintained or State-aided educational institution on grounds only of religion, race, caste or language.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: Article 29(1) protects the language, script or culture of any distinct section of citizens, and Article 29(2) prohibits denial of admission on the specified grounds. Article 29 is not confined exclusively to minorities.
accepted.tq: Separate the broad protection under Article 29 from the minority-specific protection under Article 30.
accepted.sec: Articles 29-30 - language, script, culture, minority educational institutions

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes Articles 29 and 30 of the Constitution of India?
o: Article 29 applies only to minorities, whereas Article 30 applies to every section of citizens.
Article 29 deals only with religious institutions, whereas Article 30 deals only with linguistic institutions.
Article 29 concerns conservation of language, script or culture and admission protection, whereas Article 30 concerns the establishment and administration of minority educational institutions.
Both Articles 29 and 30 confer identical rights on all citizens without distinction.
accepted.x: Article 29 protects the interests of any distinct section of citizens in language, script or culture and safeguards admission. Article 30 is specifically available to religious or linguistic minorities for establishing and administering educational institutions.
accepted.tq: Use the scope comparison: Article 29 is broader, while Article 30 is minority-specific.
accepted.sec: Articles 29-30 - language, script, culture, minority educational institutions

accepted.s: Which of the following is guaranteed by Article 30(2) of the Constitution?
o: The State shall not discriminate in granting aid to educational institutions on the ground that they are under the management of a minority.
The State shall provide compulsory aid to every minority educational institution.
Minority institutions are exempt from every educational regulation.
Only linguistic minority institutions are entitled to State aid.
accepted.x: Article 30(2) prohibits discrimination in granting aid to an educational institution on the ground that it is under the management of a religious or linguistic minority.
accepted.tq: Focus on the prohibition against discriminatory aid, not on an absolute right to receive aid.
accepted.sec: Articles 29-30 - language, script, culture, minority educational institutions

accepted.s: The 44th Constitutional Amendment inserted which provision to protect a minority institution when its property is compulsorily acquired?
o: Article 32(1A)
Article 29(1A)
Article 31(1A)
Article 30(1A)
accepted.x: The 44th Amendment added Article 30(1A), providing that compulsory acquisition of property of a minority educational institution should not impair the right to establish and administer such institution.
accepted.tq: Match the amendment with the exact sub-clause rather than the neighbouring Articles on property and remedies.
accepted.sec: Articles 29-30 - language, script, culture, minority educational institutions

accepted.s: Article 30(1A) is principally intended to ensure that acquisition of property belonging to a minority educational institution does not
o: make the institution a State institution
affect the right to establish and administer the institution
remove the institution from the scope of Article 29(2)
require approval of the Election Commission
accepted.x: Article 30(1A), inserted by the 44th Amendment, protects the minority's right to establish and administer its educational institution even when its property is acquired, subject to compensation-related protection.
accepted.tq: Apply the constitutional protection to the consequence of compulsory acquisition.
accepted.sec: Articles 29-30 - language, script, culture, minority educational institutions

accepted.s: The reference made by the President to the Supreme Court in the matter of the Kerala Education Bill, 1957, was under
o: Article 131
Article 136
Article 143
Article 145
accepted.x: The Kerala Education Bill, 1957 was considered by the Supreme Court pursuant to a Presidential reference under Article 143.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the advisory jurisdiction under Article 143 from the Court's original and appellate jurisdictions.

accepted.s:
With reference to the decision in In re Kerala Education Bill, 1957, consider the following statements:
1. Minorities were recognised as having the right to establish educational institutions.
2. The State could attach reasonable conditions to the grant of aid.
3. The judgment held that minority institutions could never be regulated by the State.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: The decision recognised the right of minorities to establish institutions and accepted reasonable conditions attached to State aid. It did not grant immunity from every form of State regulation.
accepted.tq: Reject the absolute word “never” while retaining the two propositions supported by the case.

accepted.s: In St. Xavier's College v. Gujarat (1974), the Supreme Court held that regulations concerning a minority educational institution were permissible primarily for ensuring
o: State takeover of its administration
reservation of all seats for the State
standards and excellence in education
abolition of minority management
accepted.x: St. Xavier's College v. Gujarat protected the right to administer minority institutions but accepted regulations intended to maintain academic standards and educational excellence.
accepted.tq: Distinguish regulation for academic standards from interference with administration.

accepted.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: P.A. Inamdar (2005) — Presidential reference under Article 143
In re Kerala Education Bill (1957) — 11-judge Bench and State-wise minority status
St. Xavier's College v. Gujarat (1974) — right to administer protected, subject to standards and excellence regulations
T.M.A. Pai Foundation (2002) — seven-judge Bench and no State quota in unaided institutions
accepted.x: St. Xavier's College v. Gujarat held that the right to administer is protected, while regulations for standards and excellence are permissible. The other options interchange the holdings or procedural features of the cases.
accepted.tq: Find the correctly matched case and holding by separating the four landmark decisions.

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002):
1. It was decided by an 11-judge Bench.
2. Minority status is determined State-wise.
3. Unaided institutions enjoy institutional autonomy.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: T.M.A. Pai Foundation was decided by an 11-judge Bench. It held that minority status is determined with reference to the State and recognised autonomy for unaided institutions.
accepted.tq: Treat bench strength, territorial basis and institutional autonomy as separate statement checks.

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the decision in P.A. Inamdar (2005)?
o: A seven-judge Bench held that the State could impose its quota in unaided institutions without limitation.
A seven-judge Bench held that there could be no State quota or reservation in unaided institutions, contributing to the subsequent 93rd Amendment framework.
An 11-judge Bench abolished the distinction between aided and unaided institutions.
The Court held that minority status must be determined at the national level.
accepted.x: P.A. Inamdar was decided by a seven-judge Bench and held that the State could not impose its quota or reservation in unaided institutions. The decision was followed by the constitutional development associated with Article 15(5) through the 93rd Amendment.
accepted.tq: Combine bench strength, holding and constitutional consequence without confusing it with T.M.A. Pai.

accepted.s: The constitutional provision associated with the post-P.A. Inamdar development concerning reservation in educational institutions is
o: Article 19(1)(g) through the 44th Amendment
Article 14 through the 42nd Amendment
Article 30(1A) through the 86th Amendment
Article 15(5) through the 93rd Amendment
accepted.x: The development following P.A. Inamdar is associated with Article 15(5), introduced through the 93rd Constitutional Amendment.
accepted.tq: Separate the amendment linked to reservation in educational institutions from the amendments linked to property and education rights.

accepted.s: Which of the following statements correctly reflects the comparative scope of writ jurisdiction in India?
o: High Courts can issue writs only for enforcement of Fundamental Rights, whereas the Supreme Court can issue them for any legal right.
The Supreme Court and High Courts have identical writ jurisdiction in both territory and subject matter.
The Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction is wider in territorial scope than that of High Courts.

High Courts have a wider subject-matter scope because they may issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for other purposes, while the Supreme Court's Article 32 jurisdiction is for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
accepted.x: Article 32 empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights, whereas Article 226 gives High Courts wider subject-matter jurisdiction by extending it to other purposes. The Supreme Court is wider territorially, while the High Court's power is not wider in territory.
accepted.tq: Split the comparison into territorial reach and subject-matter scope.

accepted.s: The Indian constitutional writs are principally derived from the
o: American Bill of Rights
French administrative law
English prerogative writs
Roman civil law
accepted.x: The writ jurisdiction incorporated into the Indian constitutional system is derived from the English prerogative writ tradition.
accepted.tq: Recall the legal source of the writs rather than their Indian constitutional Articles.

accepted.s: The statement that “a right without a remedy is a worthless declaration” most directly explains the constitutional significance of
o: Article 30 providing aid to minority institutions
Article 143 providing advisory jurisdiction
Article 32 making Part III rights judicially enforceable
Article 29 protecting admission to aided institutions
accepted.x: Article 32 provides a direct constitutional remedy for enforcement of Fundamental Rights, thereby making the rights in Part III effective rather than merely declaratory.
accepted.tq: Connect the general principle of remedy with the constitutional mechanism that enforces rights.

accepted.s: The Supreme Court agreed on 20 January 2026 to examine whether the Enforcement Directorate can invoke writ jurisdiction in a matter involving challenges arising from
o: Kerala and Karnataka against a Bombay High Court ruling
Kerala and Tamil Nadu against a Kerala High Court ruling
West Bengal and Odisha against a Madras High Court ruling
Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh against a Delhi High Court ruling
accepted.x: On 20 January 2026, a Supreme Court Bench comprising Justices Dipankar Datta and S.C. Sharma agreed to examine the issue in appeals involving Kerala and Tamil Nadu against a Kerala High Court ruling.
accepted.tq: Use the place-and-issue pairing to distinguish the current writ-jurisdiction development.

accepted.s: Which one of the following current developments concerns the Supreme Court's examination of urgent constitutional remedies for threats to life and liberty?
o: A uniform reservation policy for all minority institutions under Article 30
An SOP for 24x7 urgent hearings under Articles 32 and 226
A constitutional amendment replacing Articles 32 and 226 with Article 131
A proposal to abolish High Court writ jurisdiction
accepted.x: The Supreme Court was examining an SOP for 24x7 urgent hearings in matters involving threats to life and liberty, strengthening practical access to remedies under Articles 32 and 226.
accepted.tq: Identify the practical remedy being examined rather than confusing it with a change in constitutional text.

accepted.s: A proposal to treat religious-instruction schools under Article 26(a), instead of Article 30(1), was left for consideration to the
o: Ministry of Law and Justice
National Commission for Minorities
Ministry of Education
Ministry of Minority Affairs exclusively
accepted.x: The plea concerning treatment of religious-instruction schools under Article 26(a) rather than Article 30(1) was left to the Ministry of Education.
accepted.tq: Apply the “which authority handles the matter?” test to distinguish the concerned ministry.

accepted.s: As of 18 September 2025, the number of High Courts mentioned in the constitutional writ-jurisdiction context, along with their sanctioned strength, was
o: 25 High Courts and 1,122 judges
26 High Courts and 1,122 judges
25 High Courts and 1,222 judges
24 High Courts and 1,122 judges
accepted.x: The stated figures were 25 High Courts and a sanctioned strength of 1,122 judges as on 18 September 2025.
accepted.tq: Check the institution count and sanctioned strength separately, especially the close numerical distractors.

accepted.s: In the ED-West Bengal matter, the constitutional issue involved a contest between
o: an Article 136 appeal by the Centre and an Article 368 reference by the State
an Article 226 petition by the Centre and an Article 143 reference by the State
an Article 32 petition defended by the Centre and an Article 131 suit claimed by the State
an Article 30 petition by the Centre and an Article 29 claim by the State
accepted.x: The Centre defended an Article 32 petition, while the State argued that the dispute should proceed as an original suit under Article 131.
accepted.tq: Distinguish enforcement of Fundamental Rights under Article 32 from intergovernmental original jurisdiction under Article 131.
